sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Continuous autoregressive TTS relies on an acoustic target that enables stable next-latent modeling while preserving fine-grained acoustic details. While existing approaches employ learned compressed representations (e.g., continuous VAE latents) to render prediction tractable, they rely on complex neural encoders that often cap generation fidelity. Conversely, training-free targets like mel-spectrograms eliminate encoder overhead, yet their potential for autoregressive generation remains largely underexplored. In this work, we propose VoxMel, a tokenizer-free framework for autoregressive TTS that makes stable mel modeling tractable through a fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar transform. The transform first decomposes each mel spectrogram along frequency into local averages and a frequency residual, then splits the averaged component along time into Coarse-Mel and a temporal residual. A language-model backbone with a flow-matching head autoregressively generates Coarse-Mel. Non-autoregressive residual tiers then predict the temporal residual from Coarse-Mel, followed by the frequency residual conditioned on the reconstructed Frequency-Averaged Mel. Neither residual is fed back into the autoregressive history. Trained on 100K hours of Emilia, the supervised 0.6B model obtains 1.51\% WER and 0.738 speaker similarity (SIM) on test-en, and 1.29\% CER and 0.755 SIM on test-zh. GRPO improves these results to 1.15\% WER / 0.753 SIM and 1.17\% CER / 0.776 SIM, respectively. We also distill the guided flow head into two- and four-step students, requiring 2 or 4 head evaluations per coarse frame. The four-step student retains competitive SIM and nearly matches the supervised model in WER/CER.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) has advanced rapidly by casting speech generation as autoregressive sequence modeling with language-model backbones (Wang et al., 2023; Du et al., 2024a; Anastassiou et al., 2024). 1 central design choice in these systems is the acoustic representation to be generated. Most existing approaches autoregress over learned, compressed representations, including discrete codec tokens (Défossez et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023) and continuous latents from trained autoencoders (Peng et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026). Consequently, synthesis quality depends in part on the learned encoder and the fidelity of its reconstruction. Mel spectrograms offer complementary alternative. As standard acoustic target in TTS (Shen et al., 2018; Ren et al., 2021), they avoid the need for learned acoustic tokenizer and remain interpretable and modelindependent. Although vocoder is still required to convert mel spectrograms into waveforms, it can be independently upgraded without retraining the autoregressive generator. Despite these advantages, mel spectrograms have received limited attention as continuous autoregressive targets (Meng et al., 2024). Direct autoregression over full-band mel spectrograms presents two challenges. Strong temporal redundancy may let model rely on acoustic history under teacher forcing instead of using the text condition. Moreover, each sampled frame, including its fine-grained details, is fed back into the history, where prediction errors may accumulate. Frame patching (Jia et al., 2025) and low-frame-rate learned latents (Peng et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026) reduce the number of autoregressive steps, but their generated patches or latents still enter the history. Token-wise coarse-to-fine methods (Wang et al., 2025a; Wu et al., 2025) likewise feed reconstructed full-band frames into later steps. We propose VoxMel, tokenizer-free TTS framework that applies fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar transform to mel spectrograms. The transform first splits the frequency axis into Frequency-Averaged Mel and frequency residual, then splits Frequency-Averaged Mel along time into compact Coarse-Mel sequence and temporal residual. language-model backbone with flow-matching head generates Coarse-Mel autoregressively. Two nonautoregressive tiers then predict the temporal residual from Coarse-Mel and the frequency residual from the reconstructed Frequency-Averaged Mel. Because neither residual enters the autoregressive history, the model generates compact coarse sequence while retaining enough information to reconstruct the complete mel spectrogram. We evaluate VoxMel on LibriSpeech and Seed-TTS-eval, including ablations of residual feedback, comparisons with other speech generation systems, and experiments on GRPO post-training and flow-head distillation. Our contributions are: Wavelet-factorized mel modeling. VoxMel applies fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar wavelet transform to mel spectrograms. language-model backbone autoregresses only over Coarse-Mel, while nonautoregressive residual tiers predict the temporal and frequency residuals in dependency order. Post-training and distillation. Frozen-head GRPO improves all four Seed-TTS-eval metrics. We also distill the guided flow head into guidance-conditioned students with two or four inference steps, reducing head evaluations per coarse frame from 96 to 2 or 4. The four-step student retains competitive SIM and nearly matches the supervised model in WER/CER. Evaluation and analysis. We evaluate zero-shot synthesis on LibriSpeech test-clean and Seed-TTS-eval test-en/test-zh. Decomposition ablations examine how removing residuals from the autoregressive history affects text reliance and end-to-end synthesis.

sections.content: Let = (x1, . . . , xT ) RT denote log-mel spectrogram with frames and mel channels, and let denote the conditioning information (text and speaker prompt). Continuous autoregressive TTS factorizes the conditional density as TY p(X y) = p(xt x<t, y) , (1) t= where language-model backbone summarizes the prefix in hidden state ht = fθ(x<t, y) and samplingbased prediction head draws xt pϕ( ht). The head may be variational latent head (Meng et al., 2024), diffusion head (Jia et al., 2025), or conditional flow-matching head that transports Gaussian noise to the target conditioned on ht (Lipman et al., 2023). Patch-based variants Jia et al. (2025); Zhou et al. (2026) group consecutive frames into one autoregressive step, with the head modeling the joint distribution of block. Training uses teacher forcing. At inference, each sampled frame or patch is fed back into the history.

sections.title: 3.1 Motivation for Coarse-Mel Autoregression
sections.content: We analyze 2,000 utterances from LibriSpeech test-clean. Adjacent mel frames have lag-one autocorrelation of 0.944. linear predictor using only the preceding frame reduces target variance by 11.3 dB (about 93%); adding more than two past frames yields only about 0.2 dB of additional gain. After the two-axis Haar split, Coarse-Mel accounts for 92.9% of the summed coeﬀicient variance but only 25% of the coeﬀicients. The temporal and frequency residuals account for 1.9% and 5.2%, respectively. The temporal residual has little autocorrelation: using its own past gives only 0.28 dB of prediction gain. Its probe R2 rises from about 0.01 with the same-position coarse coeﬀicient to 0.57 when neighboring coarse frames are included. For the frequency residual, same-frame coarse context gives probe R2 of about 0.42, with little gain from adding temporal context. These measurements motivate excluding both residuals from the autoregressive history. Section 4.4 reports ablations on trained models.

sections.title: 3.4 Architecture
sections.content: Figure 1 summarizes the data flow: the coarse stream is generated autoregressively, the residual bands are added in coarse-to-fine order, and the inverse Haar transform reconstructs the mel spectrogram. The right side of the figure expands the residual tiers and the flow-matching head used to sample each band. Autoregressive Coarse-Mel generation. The transcript is tokenized, and the text conditions are combined with projected Coarse-Mel history as input to decoder-only transformer. At each step, its hidden state conditions flow-matching head that samples the next Coarse-Mel unit; stop head predicts when to end the sequence. With frame-wise prediction, there are /2 steps, each of dimension /2half as many steps as frame-level mel generation. Inference applies separate guidance scales to text and speaker prompt conditions (Section 4.2). Residual generation and reconstruction. The temporal-residual tier uses non-autoregressive transformer and flow-matching head conditioned on Coarse-Mel. Its prediction is combined with Coarse-Mel to reconstruct Frequency-Averaged Mel, which conditions the frequency-residual tier. This second tier predicts each frame independently. Prediction is parallel within each tier but sequential across tiers. The inverse Haar transform then reconstructs the full mel spectrogram, which the vocoder converts to speech. Flow-matching head. As shown in the lower-right inset, each head takes noisy input together with the flow time and its conditioning signal (the transformer state for Coarse-Mel, or coarse-level context for residual). An MLP predicts the flow, and an ODE solver integrates it to produce Coarse-Mel unit or residual sample. Training. sections.title: 3.5 GRPO with a Frozen Flow Head
sections.content: We apply Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) after supervised training to optimize the autoregressive Coarse-Mel policy. Motivated by prior work that freezing the diffusion head can stabilize RL in autoregressivediffusion hybrids (Ma et al., 2026), we adopt this strategy for VoxMel by updating only the backbone and keeping the Coarse-Mel flow head, both residual tiers, and the vocoder frozen. This keeps the mapping from the backbones predictions to audio fixed throughout RL, isolating policy updates from changes to the acoustic decoder. We evaluate this choice in Section 4.6. 6 For each text-and-speaker prompt, we sample group of eight (G = 8) outputs using the deployment twoscale classifier-free guidance scales, rather than sampling from the unguided conditional model. Each output receives scalar reward. GRPO normalizes rewards within each prompts group to estimate relative advantages: an output is favored when it scores better than the other outputs for the same prompt. KL penalty to the supervised checkpoint limits how far the updated policy can drift. The reward design and rollout and optimization settings are detailed in Section 4.6.

sections.title: 3.6 Guided Flow-Head Distillation
sections.content: Sampling cost remains in the Coarse-Mel autoregressive loop. Each coarse frame requires an ODE solve of the flow head. With two-scale guidance, each solver step requires three forward passes, corresponding to the three condition states described in Section 3.4 (full dropout schedule in Section 4.2). Thus, solver steps require 3S head evaluations per coarse frame. The guidance factor of three is removable because guidance is deterministic function of the conditional and dropped-condition velocities. We distill few-step student head that absorbs guidance into its own weights: it matches 4-step guided teacher trajectory while taking the guidance scales (ωtext, ωspk) as explicit inputs, sampled during training from ranges spanning the useful operating region. At inference the student uses the requested scales and one conditional forward pass per solver step, thereby avoiding separate dropped-condition passes while keeping the scales tunable without retraining. Distillation starts from the GRPO checkpoint and updates only the head, with the backbone and tiers fixed. We draw fraction of training batches from the students own rollouts, so the head trains on the conditioning it will meet at inference rather than on groundtruth prefixes alone; without this the distilled head degrades severely (Section 4.7).

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We first report benchmark and model-scaling results, then evaluate GRPO post-training and sampling eﬀiciency, and finally test transfer to DiTAR-style backbone. Decomposition ablations and their mechanism probes are in Section 4.4.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: We evaluate three VoxMel sizes (0.15B, 0.3B, and 0.6B), which share the same wavelet target and training data but vary in backbone and tier configuration. Unless stated otherwise, results are for VoxMel-0.6B. Architecture and model sizes. The backbone is initialized from Qwen2.5-0.5B and used as feature extractor. Table 2 reports the 0.6B module counts; Table 3 lists all three sizes. The temporal residual tier uses bidirectional attention, while the frequency tier processes each frame independently. Data and acoustic front-end. We train on 100K hours of Emilia (He et al., 2024), discarding utterances shorter than 0.3 or longer than 30 s. Batches use budget of 24,000 frames and maximum sequence length of 4096 tokens. We use the Qwen2.5 tokenizer. The target is 100-channel log-mel spectrogram at 24 kHz, computed with an FFT/window size of 1024 and hop of 256 samples (93.75 frames/s); frozen Vocos vocoder reconstructs 24-kHz waveforms. Optimization and inference. We use AdamW with learning rate 2104, cosine decay, and 10,000 warmup steps. The supervised 0.6B checkpoint is taken after 900,000 steps. sections.title: 4.3 Benchmark Results
sections.content: On Seed-TTS-eval test-en, supervised VoxMel-0.6B obtains 1.51% WER and 0.738 SIM, compared with 1.69% and 0.735 for DiTAR and 1.70% and 0.697 for ZipVoice  (Table 1)  . On test-zh, VoxMel obtains 1.29% CER and 0.755 SIM. Several systems have lower CER, while the GRPO variant improves VoxMels results to 1.15% WER / 0.753 SIM on test-en and 1.17% CER / 0.776 SIM on test-zh. On LibriSpeech test-clean, VoxMel-0.6B obtains 1.98% WER and 0.721 SIM; GRPO changes these to 1.95% and 0.736. The GRPO model has the highest SIM in the table, while its WER remains above OmniVoiceEmilia (1.57%) and VoxCPM (1.74%). We also compared VoxMel with four baselines in five-point listening test. VoxMels naturalness/similarity scores are 3.89/3.97 in Chinese and 3.96/4.11 in English. The highest scores vary by system and metric; Table 4 reports means and 95% confidence intervals. Listening protocol. Twenty native speakers per language rated naturalness and speaker similarity on separate five-point scales. Naturalness raters heard synthesized clip with its text; similarity raters compared reference and synthesized clips while judging voice identity independently of content and recording quality.

sections.title: 4.5 Model Scaling
sections.content: From 0.15B to 0.6B, English WER falls from 1.90% to 1.51%, and speaker similarity rises from 0.667 to 0.738 on test-en and from 0.730 to 0.755 on test-zh. Chinese CER is lowest at 1.17% for the 0.3B model; it is 1.44% for the 0.15B model and 1.29% for the 0.6B model  (Table 6)  .

sections.title: 4.6 GRPO Post-Training
sections.content: We compare two GRPO variants initialized from the same supervised 0.6B checkpoint. Both update the backbone and use identical guided rollouts, rewards, and optimization settings. The trainable-head variant also updates the Coarse-Mel flow head, whereas the frozen-head variant keeps it fixed; the residual tiers remain frozen in both. We sample eight guided rollouts per prompt and combine speaker similarity with ASR-based transcription accuracy using equal reward weights. Advantages are normalized within each group, with KL penalty (β = 0.01) to the supervised checkpoint. Rollouts use 10 Euler steps, injected noise σ = 0.15, and learning rate 2 106. GRPO uses 10,000 Emilia examples for 1,000 updates. After 1,000 GRPO steps, the frozen-head variant improves all four Seed-TTS-eval metrics over the supervised baseline: test-en WER falls from 1.51% to 1.15% and SIM rises from 0.738 to 0.753; test-zh CER falls from 1.29% to 1.17% and SIM rises from 0.755 to 0.776. The trainable-head variant performs worse than both the frozen-head variant and the supervised baseline on all four metrics  (Table 7)  .

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Mel as synthesis target. Before language-model-based speech generation, mel spectrograms were standard acoustic target for TTS systems such as Tacotron 2, Transformer-TTS, and FastSpeech 2. These systems predict mel features and rely on separate vocoder to synthesize waveforms (Shen et al., 2018; Li et al., 2019; Ren et al., 2021). VoxMel retains mels interpretable, tokenizer-free representation, but changes how it is used autoregressively: only the coarse wavelet component, rather than the full frame, enters the history. Learned speech representations. Many zero-shot TTS systems instead generate learned audio representations, including discrete codec tokens and continuous latents. This line of work spans AudioLM and VALL-E (Borsos et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023), as well as the CosyVoice, IndexTTS, and FireRedTTS families (Du et al., 2024a,b, 2025; Deng et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025). The representations range from residual and scalar quantization (Défossez et al., 2022; Kumar et al., 2023; Mentzer et al., 2024) to decoupled token streams (Wang et al., 2025b) and end-to-end learned latents (Zhou et al., 2026). In contrast to these learned representations, VoxMel applies fixed, invertible coarseresidual transform directly to mel features. Continuous generation and history robustness. MAR provides related precedent in image generation, using per-step diffusion head to generate continuous image patches rather than discrete tokens (Li et al., 2024). Speech models employ related generative heads, but differ from MAR in both architecture and target representation. MELLE and FELLE autoregress directly over mel-spectrogram frames, using variational sampling and flow matching, respectively. ARDiT, DiTAR, and CLEAR instead model learned continuous acoustic latents; these systems use learned autoencoder-based representations, including VAEs (Meng et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2024; Jia et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). VibeVoice also uses low-rate 12 learned acoustic latents (Peng et al., 2025). These models differ in what enters the autoregressive history. DiTAR feeds generated latent patches into later steps, while MELLE and FELLE feed back generated mel frames; FELLEs within-step refinement does not change that feedback. VoxMel instead keeps its residual bands out of the history. Non-autoregressive flow and diffusion models avoid this recursion altogether (Le et al., 2023; Shen et al., 2024; Guan et al., 2024; Eskimez et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2025). Multiscale factorization. Prior hierarchical speech models learn their coarse-to-fine structure: HALL-E and MARS6 use layered codecs at different temporal rates, while HAM-TTS adds learned acoustic hierarchy over tokens (Nishimura et al., 2025; Baas et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024). VoxMel instead obtains its levels from fixed Haar transform. This linear split is exactly invertible and adds no trainable parameters; we use it to keep the coarse component in the autoregressive history and generate the residuals separately.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: VoxMel offers learned-tokenizer-free approach to autoregressive mel-spectrogram modeling. fixed, exactly invertible two-axis Haar transform separates coarse sequence from temporal and frequency residuals. The model feeds only the coarse sequence into its autoregressive history and predicts the residuals in separate non-autoregressive tiers, preserving the full mel representation without autoregressive residual feedback. Our experiments show that this factorization encourages greater reliance on text than full-band mel autoregression while supporting effective zero-shot synthesis. Frozen-head GRPO further improves synthesis quality. Few-step distillation reduces sampling cost while retaining transcription accuracy close to the supervised model and competitive speaker similarity. Together, these results show that separating coarse structure from residual detail is practical way to model mel-spectrograms autoregressively.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Depth and choice of transform. We use one Haar split per axis, motivated by the measured first-order temporal redundancy. We do not evaluate alternative depths, other wavelet families in this work. Languages and speech styles. We evaluate English and Chinese on benchmarks of single-speaker utterances few seconds long. Tonal languages beyond Chinese, richer morphology, languages requiring specialized text front ends, long-form synthesis, multi-speaker dialogue, expressive and paralinguistic control, singing, and code-switching are all outside this evaluation. Other audio domains. Our evaluation is limited to speech. Although the Haar transform itself is not speechspecific, we have not tested whether its subband structure or the proposed autoregressive factorization is effective for music, general audio, or sound effects. Evaluating these domains, as well as alternative timefrequency representations, remains future work.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: VoxMel supports zero-shot voice cloning from reference speech, which may enable impersonation, nonconsensual voice synthesis, or attempts to spoof speaker-verification systems. Any release should document training data provenance and consent, define acceptable uses, and consider safeguards such as output watermarking and evaluated synthetic-speech detection.
